utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can the case be called, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-82-PT, The Prosecutor versus Ljube Boskoski and Johan Tarculovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Chamber is sitting today as part of its pre-trial preparation for the trial of this case. The Chamber specifically indicated through its officers that there was no need for counsel to attend. The record would reveal the matters we were dealing with. Nevertheless, we're delighted to see that some counsel has taken the trouble to be here. Mr. Saxon, you appear for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, together with my colleague Ms. Joanne Motoike.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Presiding Judge, I am Edina Residovic and I defend the interest the Mr. Boskoski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, the Chamber, as presently constituted, has now been formerly pointed both to complete pre-trial matters and from the 12th of April to conduct the trial. There were early orders of Judge Agius as Presiding Judge of Trial Chamber II in respect of the pre-trial composition of the Chamber, and they have now been supplemented by two orders of the President of the 30th of March, and one of Judge Agius of the 2nd of April. Strictly, between the 30th of March and the 2nd of April, there were four Judges constituting the Pre-Trial Chamber because Judge Agius was still a member. That was corrected by his order of the 2nd of April. To ensure there is no confusion, we now confirm the six Rule 92 bis and 92 ter decisions and the decision on protective measures that were issued on Friday, the 30th of March, 2007. It was felt important that they issue to give the parties as much notice and time as possible. The Chamber, having been constituted now with a view to conducting the trial, there are a number of other motions that are relevant to the preparation and conduct of the trial, and it is important for all concerned that these be dealt with and decided as quickly as possible. We propose today to deal in brief oral decisions with six, strictly speaking seven, of those motions. The remaining ones are more complex and there will be written decisions delivered in the near future, and I find that even now more motions are coming in. We will do our best against the movement of the tide. The first of the decisions that we deliver today is in respect of the Prosecution's motion for permission to add additional exhibits to its first amended exhibit list with confidential annexes A to E, which was filed on the 16th of January, 2007. The Boskoski Defence has responded, no responses has been made by the Tarculovski Defence, and there was a reply by the Prosecution. The Prosecution seeks to add four documents to its first amended exhibit list which was filed on the 31st of March, 2006. The Boskoski Defence opposes this. The first amended exhibit list was filed pursuant to an order of the then Pre-Trial Chamber that the Prosecution should do so no later than 31st of March, 2006. Now, the four documents are document 989, a photograph of the dead body of one of the victims alleged to be a victim of one of the charges of murder in the indictment. It is intended that this photograph be tendered through a Prosecution witness. The photograph was disclosed to the Defence on the 16th of August, 2006. It is submitted by the Prosecution that it was accidently omitted from its first amended exhibit list. The second document is 990, a record of permissions issued by the Macedonian government to the Office of the Prosecutor for access to classified information. Part of this document is also a list of documents scanned from various archives of the Ministry of Interior which were included in the Prosecution's first amended exhibit list. This document was disclosed to the Defence on the 31st of March, 2006, but inadvertently omitted from its first amended exhibit list. The Prosecution regards this document as relevant to establishing both the authenticity and the chain of custody of documents included in its list. The third is document 991, a list of documents provided by the Macedonian government to the Office of the Prosecutor in March 2006. Many of these documents are included in the first amended exhibit list. Document 991 appears to have been disclosed on the 16th of January, 2007. Again, the Prosecution would rely on this as relevant to establishing the authenticity and the chain of custody of other documents. Document 992 contains annexes to the witness statement of an intended witness, Mr. Bouckert. It is proposed to be tendered through that witness. These documents were not included in the first amended exhibit list due to oversight. They were included -- sorry, they were disclosed to the Defence on the 28th of April, 2006 in English and on the 23rd of May, 2006 in Macedonian. The same documents are also the subject of a separate Prosecution motion to allow additional attachments to the written statement of Mr. Bouckert, which was filed on the 12th of January 2007. As the submissions are in fact identical, the Chamber will deal with this issue in the context of this decision and this motion and will regard the motion of the 12th of January, 2007 as mute. This is the seventh motion to which I adverted when saying that we will be giving six decisions. Finally, in the motion, the Prosecution clarify that a fifth document, being minutes of a meeting of the 12th of November, 2003 of a commission investigating events in Ljuboten, was in fact already included on its exhibit list and, therefore, no leave to add this document was sought, contrary to what had been earlier indications of the Prosecution. The Boskoski Defence opposes the motion on the grounds that these documents should have been included in the first amended list and that good cause has not been demonstrated, arguing that mere oversight or omission is not a good cause. It is also said that the addition of these documents will cause prejudice, and it questions the relevance of the documents 991 and 992. At the outset, relevant both to this motion and other motions to be dealt with today, we would emphasise there is a difference between the admission of a document into evidence as an exhibit and the inclusion of a document into the Rule 65 list. The purpose of the list is to give notice to the Defence, that Prosecution intends to rely on the document. This notice allows the Defence to prepare its case accordingly. In some cases, it will be clear that a proposed exhibit is obviously irrelevant and that it will not admitted for that or for some other reason. Where that is clear, it is in everyone's interest that the Chamber decide this pre-trial to exclude that document from the case and to avoid the need for time to be wasted on it in preparation. In many cases, however, the issues affecting the admissibility of a proposed exhibit are not clear or are disputed. In those cases, it is usually necessary to defer decision about the admission of the document until the relevant evidence is placed before the Chamber. If there is then an objection to its admission, that objection can be the subject of a decision which is reached on the basis of the actual relevant evidence, not simply on disputed submissions of counsel. The documents which the Prosecution now seeks to add to its Rule 65 ter list by this motion appear to be relevant to or to provide more detail of the Prosecution case. These documents were disclosed to the Defence in August 2006, March 2006, April 2006, May 2006, and January 2007 respectively. That is well before the start of the trial. The motion concerns only four out of almost one thousand documents the Prosecution intends to tender during the trial. In the view of the Chamber, the Defence will have sufficient time to prepare its Defence with respect to these documents. No prejudice will be caused to the Defence if these documents are added to the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter list, even though this is after the deadline prescribed by the Pre-Trial Chamber last year. Despite the failure of the Prosecution in these respects to meet its obligations of timeliness, it is in the Chamber's view understandable that a few documents were overlooked, given the number to be considered so that we feel there is good cause sufficiently demonstrated. The Chamber therefore grants the motion. The second motion concerns a second expert report by Dr. Simon Eichner with an annex, the motion having been filed on the 30th of January, 2007. Only the Boskoski Defence responded. There were two further Prosecution replies and a further Defence response because of an issue that rather distracted the attention of counsel for some time. On the 30th of the January this year, the Prosecution submitted a second expert report from Dr. Simon Eichner. He is from the Bavarian State Institute of Criminology. The Prosecution submits it has both relevance and probative value to its case insofar as it relies on joint criminal enterprise, to the charge of murder, and to the issue of the measures undertaken by the Macedonian police to investigate the events in Ljuboten. The Prosecution indicates that it requested assistance in respect of these matters to the government of Macedonian on the 11th of July, 2005, seeking to be provided with three fire-arms said to be seized at Ljuboten on the 12th of August, 2001, which is the first of the three days the subject of the specific charges in the indictment. These weapons were transported to Germany for analysis by Dr. Eichner on the 18th of May, 2006. His report was not completed until the 15th of January, 2007, and that report was disclosed to the Defence some few days later, on the 24th of January. The Boskoski Defence opposes the application, submitting that the Prosecution has failed to comply about the deadline of the disclosure of the expert reports which was also the 31st of March, 2006; that the report irrelevant and unnecessarily would prolong the proceedings; further, that is correct until the 24th of January this year, they had no notice that such a report had been requested; and that it took the OTP, the Office of the Prosecutor, more than five and a half years to obtain the report. In this last respect, the Chamber would mention that the indictment was only confirmed on the 9th of March, 2005. No action of that type could reasonably have been expected until after that, and the Prosecution then acted, in this respect, within four months of that confirmation. A preliminary procedural question was raised by the Defence that the Prosecution's reply introduced new arguments not included in their main submission. It was said they included matters not included in the indictment and the pre-trial brief and of which the Defence had no notice. The Prosecution in replying to this relies on and further clarified an argument made when it initially submitted the report. This sufficiently demonstrated, in the Chamber's view, that there is no new argument or issue, and it also demonstrated the relevance. There is no reason, therefore, for the Prosecution's request for leave to file a reply to be denied. On analysis, it is sufficiently apparent that the report is both relevant to and could offer support to the Prosecution's original case, which is that the Macedonian police force -- police forced ethnic Albanian residents of Ljuboten to sign certain fire-arm seizure records under coercion, to indicate that those persons had been in possession of fire-arms and ammunition when in fact the fire-arms had actually been seized by the police from another location. The Prosecution case is that this is capable of revealing the real object of the alleged joint criminal enterprise; that is, to direct an unlawful attack on civilians and civilian objects in the village of Ljuboten, an attack not justified by military necessity, which is, of course, the subject of a specific charge in the current indictment. Having regard to those matters, the Chamber is of the view that the report has apparent probative value. Although it is clearly out of the time fixed for expert reports, the circumstances show a sufficient good cause within Rule 127. It is the view of the Chamber that the interests of justice favour the report being the subject of evidence when Dr. Eichner is called as has always been intended. This will, therefore, be allowed by the Chamber. The third motion is one in which the Prosecution sought leave to add (redacted), Dr. Jacovski and (redacted), to the proposed second amended witness list and also to have leave to remove two witnesses, one Georgievski and Ramadani, with annexes A to C from that list. The motion was filed on the 1st of March this year. There has been a response from the Boskoski Defence and a reply by the Prosecution. The two additional witnesses are a forensic pathologist, Dr. Jacovski, and (redacted), who, it is submitted, will provide a mixture of both fact and expert evidence about injuries allegedly suffered by victims named in the indictment. Dr. Jacovski conducted the autopsy on one of the victims, and the Prosecution seek to rely on his evidence as relevant to establishing the existence of the joint criminal enterprise alleged, that the crimes charged with a natural and foreseeable consequences of that joint criminal enterprise, that the victim was murdered as alleged in the indictment, and that residents of Ljuboten were subjected to beatings and other forms of cruel treatment as alleged in the indictment. (redacted) examined two people who had been detained by the police and brought by them to the Skopje city hospital from Ljuboten on the 13th of August, 2001. They are both named in the indictment as victims of cruel treatment. Her proposed evidence, as indicated in the report, deals with the injuries of these two detainees. The proposed evidence also suggests that unknown persons altered records that she produced with respect to these two detainees by typing through words of hers "hit by the police" and in other respects. The Prosecution would seek to rely on this evidence with reference to the existence of the alleged joint criminal enterprise, the allegations of cruel treatment, and also the allegations that an adequate investigation was not conducted. The Prosecution had requested the assistance of the authorities of Macedonia to contact these two witnesses only in January 2007. It interviewed and took signed statements from them in February and Dr. Jacovski's statement was disclosed on the 16th of February and (redacted). (redacted) on the 23rd of February, 2007. The Boskoski Defence opposes the motion to add these two witnesses on the grounds that the proposed evidence is not relevant, a violation of the time fixed for the disclosure of the statements of expert witnesses, and that the Prosecution has not acted with due diligence, and that it would be prejudiced, in particular, by the need for additional investigation and preparation. The Prosecution as a preliminary matter notes that the Boskoski Defence response was filed out of time. In the Chamber's view, the two proposed witnesses, at least in part, are expert witnesses and, therefore, the 30-day deadline provided by Rule 94 bis should apply, and on that basis the Defence response was within time. The Rules of Procedure and Evidence do not directly govern the present situation. Rule 73 bis (E) actually permits the Prosecution, even after the commencement of a trial, to file a motion to vary the number of witnesses that are to be called, and this may be allowed where it is in the interests of justice to do so. The Chamber will approach the present motion on that same basis. Of course, the requirements for the admissibility of evidence are relevance and probative value in accordance with Rule 89(C). Further, in accessing where the interests of justice lie in respect of this motion, the Chamber must consider whether the contemplative probative value of the evidence would be substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial, in particular whether the interests of the Defence will be adequately protected. The proposed witnesses are doctors who have examined victims shortly after they received injuries that are alleged in the indictment. The proposed evidence is, therefore, apparently relevant and apparently of probative value. The expert statements were disclosed on the 16th of February and the 23rd of February of this year respectively. Earlier than that, copies of the report of the autopsy conducted by Dr. Jacovski on the same victim as is the subject of his expert report was disclosed to the Defence as early as the 7th of November, 2005. Further, while in December 2006 the Prosecution and the Boskoski Defence were able to agree as to the fact of death of several residents in Ljuboten, no agreement was reached with respect to the person the subject of Dr. Jacovski's evidence. A similar agreement was reached between the Prosecution and the Tarculovski Defence in February 2007, again, not with reference to this alleged victim. With respect to (redacted), it appears that the Prosecution sought the assistance of the Macedonian authorities to view medical records at the Skopje city hospital pertaining, among others, to the two persons that are the subject of her proposed report and also to interview (redacted) on the 29th of January this year. Similar requests for assistance with access to these records had been filed twice in 2003, but there had been no response from the Macedonian government. In view of the fact that in the case of Dr. Jacovski an autopsy report pertaining to the same victim was written and disclosed to the Defence in November 2005, and that the possibility of an agreement about death was clearly being explored near the end of 2006, although unsuccessfully, the Chamber is persuaded that there exists good cause for the late filing of Dr. Jacovski's report, further considering that efforts had been made by the Prosecution to obtain the hospital records upon which (redacted) new report are based, is based and had sought to obtain those as early as 2003. The Prosecution is also satisfied that good cause exists for the late filing of her expert statements as this information was not in fact obtained from the Macedonian government until early this year. Turning next to the issue of prejudice to the Defence, the two proposed reports have been disclosed to the Defence approximately two months before the anticipated start of the trial. The Defence has been on notice of the expected evidence of Dr. Jacovski since November 2005. In light of these matters, in the view of the Chamber, the rights of the accused will not be prejudiced, so long as there is sufficient time to prepare the Defence in respect of these additional statements. It appears that this could well be achieved if there is more time before the evidence of the proposed two witnesses is heard. The Chamber notes they are not listed as early Prosecution witnesses. Of course, if more time than this is needed, this can be sought. With respect to the motion insofar as it seeks the deletion of two existing witnesses from the list, there is no opposition and there appears no reason why this should not be granted. For these reasons, this motion is granted. The fourth motion is that of the Boskoski Defence, dated the 8th of March this year, in respect of Rule 68 compliance. The Defence submits that most of the material disclosed by the Prosecution, pursuant to Rule 68, falls outside the scope of the rule and is often irrelevant to the charges. I say this was first raised as long ago as April 2006 at a Rule 65 ter hearing. Following a request from the Defence, the Prosecution had provided the Defence with a list of 148 search criteria which was used for the purpose of identifying potential Rule 68 material. That having been done, the Defence asked the Prosecution to give an indication of the steps taken by the Prosecution to review that material, and it did so twice, in January and February of this year, but the Prosecution had not responded and declined to do so. In essence, what the Defence is saying, in the Chamber's view, is that the Prosecution cannot satisfy its Rule 68 obligation by merely dumping material on to the Defence and leaving it to the Defence to identify the relevant documents, and they seek a number of orders directed to precluding the Prosecution from following the course it has been following in this respect. For its part, the Prosecution submits that it has fully complied with its Rule 68 obligations and, in particular, has actively reviewed the material in its possession to identify material that should be disclosed. It says that it commence the Rule 68 disclosure in December 2005, that it has performed electronic searches of nearly 65.000 documents, of which just over 5.000 were then passed to the trial team for further review; and of those over 5.000 documents, only 2.895 were selected as falling within Rule 68, and these are the documents that have been disclosed to the Defence. Most of them being disclosed by the 31st of March, 2006. The Prosecution further submits that each disclosure under Rule 68 has been accompanied by a detailed list describing the contents of the enclosed material. Further, when potentially exculpatory material has been provided to the Office of the Prosecutor on a confidential basis, the Prosecutor has pursued attempts to obtain the provider's consent to disclosure, as the rules contemplate. The Prosecution, in the Chamber's view, correctly also distinguishes in its submission this case from the ICTR Appeals Judgement in the Karemera case, which was relied on by the Defence, where it was made clear that the Prosecution should not bury relevant material in the middle of large amounts of irrelevant material, but should instead make the relevant material reasonably accessible. Now, Rule 68 imposes an ongoing obligation on the Prosecution to disclose exculpatory material to the Defence. In the jurisprudence, this material has been defined as material which is known to the Prosecution and is favourable to the accused in the sense that it tends to suggest the innocence or mitigate the guilt of the accused or may affect the credibility of Prosecution evidence. It is clear from this that the primary obligation lies with the Prosecution. The reality is that a vast amount of material must be reviewed by the Prosecution in any case, and that the rules impose an active obligation on the Prosecution to conduct that review. However, the rules require that material be disclosed that tends to suggest innocence or mitigate guilt, or which calls in question the credibility of Prosecution evidence so that it is inevitable if the Prosecution is conscientiously performing its role, that it will tend to err in favour of disclosure in cases where the issue is not clear whether material is exculpatory or not. The result is that often material that is disclosed may not prove to be exculpatory to the Defence as it pursues its preparation for trial or it may not further the lines of Defence which the Defence has chosen to pursue at the trial. That can be so, even though the material in the eyes of the Prosecution is such that it could be exculpatory. In the present case, it appears to the Chamber that the Prosecution has made an active effort to review the material and has dramatically narrowed the material potentially identified. While the Boskoski Defence seem to disagree with the Prosecution as to whether some of this or much of this material is in truth exculpatory, there is no basis in the material before the Chamber for the Chamber to conclude that the Prosecution is not appropriately fulfilling its obligations under the rule. We would add, of course, that the accused has a right to adequate time to prepare his Defence. If it is the case that ongoing disclosure of Rule 68 material provides a genuine hindrance to the accused's preparation of their Defence, it's open to the Defence to raise the issue and, if necessary, to seek more time to enable the Defence to be prepared. For these reasons, this motion is dismissed. We next turn to the Prosecution's fifth motion for leave to add exhibits to its first amended exhibit list, with confidential annexes A to F which was filed on the 9th of March, 2007 and which has been the subject of responses from both Defence teams. The Prosecution seeks to add 14 exhibits to a list. Five of these were obtained during an interview with the forensic physician who is an intended witness, and they deal with details and particulars of the injuries to various witnesses. They were disclosed to the Defence in Macedonian on the 23rd of February this year and in English on the 5th of March, although one document, 993, appears only to have been disclosed in Macedonian. The Boskoski Defence questions the relevance of four of these documents; they being 993, 4, 6, and 7. Two of the documents relate to the exhumation of ten bodies that are alleged to be victims form the Ljuboten village. One of these includes a set of some 293 photographs taken during the exhumation and subsequent autopsies. The other is a letter from the director of a forensic institute responsible for this exhumation, and the autopsies are dealing with those circumstances. They were disclosed to the Defence on the 23rd of February and the 9th of March respectively; and in respect to them, the Boskoski against submits that they would be simply redundant and therefore not relevant. Document 1.000 is a report by the public Prosecutor of Macedonia about the events in Ljuboten between the 10th and 14th of August, 2001. Document 1001 is a report from Dr. Jacovski, whom we've mentioned earlier, to the public Prosecutor about attempts he made between the 12th and 15th of August, 2001 to inspect the location where the bodies were found. These two documents were obtained from the Macedonian authorities and were disclosed to the Defence in November 2005 and December 2005 respectively. Again, the Boskoski Defence submits that these are not relevant, and that they may even suggest that the Prosecution is presenting a new conspiracy theory. Three documents, 1002, 3, and 4, are Skopje city hospital records for three patients who are alleged victims of the crimes. They were disclosed on the 23rd of February and the 5th and 9th of March of this year. Once again, it is submitted by the Boskoski that these are irrelevant and redundant. The remaining two documents, 1006 and 7, are records of telephone calls to and from two mobile phones alleged to have belonged to the accused Tarculovski and another intended witness in this case. These were disclosed to the Defence on the 9th of March 2006 in the most part, although a part of document 1007 was not disclosed until the 9th of March, 2007. Both Defences challenge the relevance of these documents and argue there is no evidence that these telephones belonged to these two persons. It is also contended that there's been a failure to comply with time deadlines, failure to show good cause, a failure to act with due diligence, that the application is untimely, and that amendments at this stage would cause delays and prejudice. The short statement earlier of the subject matter of the documents, in the Chamber's view, is sufficient to indicate that there is a clear potential relevance to each of the proposed documents, although it is true that in one or two cases the issue will need to be finally determined when and if the documents come to be tendered in light of the precise evidence that is offered in support or in respect of those documents. The documents in many cases have been long disclosed to the Defence, so that in substantial part, at least, they can be expected to have been included in the Defence preparation to this time it. In any event, they have been disclosed in each case before the trial and at a time when it can be expected that there will be no prejudice to the Defence if these documents are added to the Prosecution's exhibit list, especially as in nearly every case the documents relate to witnesses that appear to be down the intended list of Prosecution witnesses. The motion will therefore be granted. The last motion is one for the exclusion of proposed Prosecution exhibits and for protection of the rights of the accused, and it was filed on the 16th of March this year and this has now been a response from the Boskoski Defence and a reply from the Prosecution. The Prosecution submits that a large number of the exhibits including in the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter list are irrelevant, redundant, or so remotely irrelevant that the Chamber should exclude them. It submitted that some exhibits have been listed two or three times and some refer to issues not in dispute and that some allege or seek to prove a joint criminal enterprise of a type which goes beyond that pleaded in the indictment, such as to suggest that the Prosecution is intending to broaden the scope of its case. It is it further submitted that the Prosecution has intentionally maintained on its list exhibits which have no relevance so as to cause prejudice to the Defence. It's also complained that some exhibits have not yet been translated or not translated fully, and that many are repetitive or cumulative or that they are merely general background material to the point of irrelevance, redundancy, or simple cumulativeness. The Prosecution responds that the documents are both relevant and probative. It points out that at the request of the Boskoski Defence in February of this year, it had reviewed 637 documents on the list; that is, some 60 per cent of the proposed exhibits, and that as a consequence of that review it had removed 17 of them, and that it had provided the Defence with the table identifying each exhibit, its description, and the relevance that was intended for it. It has also in response to queries from the Boskoski Defence identified relevant parts of some large exhibits to assist the Defence in their consideration of those exhibits. If the Chamber could quickly mention some of the following matters that deal with some of the specific submissions that can be found in the submissions of the Defence. It seems that in the case of document 264 it is in fact the same as document 162, and that document 241 is in fact the same as document 252, and that Prosecution therefore seeks leave to remove in each case one of those duplicated documents. Leave is granted; otherwise, it is submitted there is no duplication in the sense that it's been submitted. The Defence made much, it is submitted, of certain documents that could have no relevance that had been in paragraph -- that were set out in paragraph 25 of the motion. They are in fact no longer on the current list, and the Chamber won't deal further with those. The Prosecution accepts that documents relevant to Boskoski's position as Minister of the Interior, a fact which is not in dispute, are also relevant to other issues in the case, such as his effective control over subordinates and over security measures in Macedonia, and therefore are properly in the list for those other purposes. The Chamber also accepts that documents relating to a mine incident, which itself is not in dispute, are relevant to other legal and factual issues in the case. The documents which the Defence were concerned were seeking by stealth, as it were, to extend the scope of the alleged of the joint criminal enterprise, are in fact in the Prosecution's contention, which the Chamber finds persuasive, they are relevant to understand the events at the time, and in this context some of them pre-date and some post-date the actual joint criminal enterprise that is relied on. Further, while some exhibits viewed on their own may be of doubtful, if any, relevance, if they are viewed in conjunction with other exhibits, a relevance becomes apparent, so that the criticisms that some of these exhibits have no possible relevance may not be accepted. There is a dispute as to the relevance of documents pertaining to terrorism charges, but these appear to have a relevance to the issue of accused Boskoski's liability under Article 7(3), as they could prove that the only charges concerning people in Ljuboten were against ethnic Albanians, and that these charges allege that they were involved in terrorist activities; that, in turn, being relevant to the question of armed conflict as one looks at all the components of that element. Separately, there is a challenge to exhibits which the Prosecution contends were relevant to the armed conflict issue. In the Chamber's view, each can be seen to have a relevance to different elements of armed conflict in the context of this case, and therefore there is a sufficient relevance to those documents. Some witness statements that are objected to are identified as sources for an expert report upon which the Prosecution proposes to rely and that therefore is sufficient to establish their relevance in this case. It is submitted by the Defence that exhibits pertaining to two military units of the Macedonian army known as the Lions And Tigers have no relevance; and in the view of the Chamber, it is clear on the materials that the nature of the military units active in the vicinity of Ljuboten at the times relevant to the indictment are of relevance in the case, and that the two units mentioned are the subject of differing and disputed evidence, so that that is a live issue in the case. In this respect, while the Chamber notes the Defence objection that it is not pleaded in the indictment that these two units were present, in the Chamber's respectful view, it is not necessary for pleading to deal with such matters of particular. There is concern by the Defence that documents which are laws and regulations are not relevant, but these appear to have a potential relevance to the liability or responsibility of the accused Boskoski under Article 7(3) and also in some respects to the existence of an armed conflict. There is objection that the inclusion of the constitution of Macedonian at the time is of no relevance, but the simple answer is that the Prosecution relies on these to demonstrate that the constitutional rights of alleged victims have been violated. There are also a number of documents pertaining to the structure of the army which are, in particular, irrelevant as sources relied upon by the proposed expert witness, Mr. Bezruchenko. We turn to the question of English translations. It is submitted by the Defence that many are missing. The Prosecution identifies that of the 75 documents so identified, only four of them are not in Macedonian, so that the provision of English translations is not a primary need for the Defence preparation, but of course will be important for the practical conduct of the trial. Of those that are originally in Macedonian, six have been translated to English and have been provided, and the relevant portions of 16 more have been provided to the Defence. A further nine documents are the subject at the moment of translation, and a further four will be translated as soon as possible. It appears that all the remaining documents in this category are those relied on by the expert -- potential expert, Bezruchenko, and there is a motion to be determined by this Chamber whether or not that witness will be permitted to testify, which is a matter of objection by the Defence. Until that motion is determined, it really is premature to be looking at the question of translation of materials which he may use as basic reference material. In summary, the Prosecution submits, except where otherwise indicated, that all these documents are relevant and/or are directly relied upon by witnesses which the Prosecution intends to call. In this context, however, the Prosecution does seek leave to remove one document, 607, as it related to a witness which the Prosecution will no longer call, and that three of these documents, 175, 190, and 615, are in truth, as the Defence identifies, repetitive. Leave is granted to remove those four documents. In this motion, we would repeat, without doing so literally, the general comments we made at the beginning about the difference between the question of the inclusion of a document on the Rule 65 ter list, and the actual admission of that document into evidence during the trial and we would remind counsel that this motion deals only with inclusion into the list, and a number of the matters dealt with in this decision on the basis of the materials presently available to the Chamber may need to be reviewed again in the trial, if and when the Prosecution should actually move for their admission when they will be considered in light of the actual evidence. In the view of the Chamber, it would be in the interests of justice, and is in the interests of justice, that these documents remain in the list of the Prosecution so that the Defence is properly on notice of them, and except the extent that we have specifically indicated, the Chamber sees no basis for their current removal and subject to the few identified matters. The motion is therefore dismissed. As a separate matter, the Chamber would make a formal order for CLSS to translate the transcript of today's hearing into Macedonian for the needs of the Defence, as today we don't have actual viva Macedonian translation into place. The Chamber would like to refer to one further motion, which is that of the Boskoski Defence filed on the 2nd of April to stop the Prosecution's continued investigation of this case and its continued disclosure. The Chamber raises it because it clearly -- this is a motion of some urgency, and it raises it to invite the Prosecution to file a response by the 10th of April, unless there is some practical impossibility about that matter. You will realise that if it is filed by the 10th of April, it would give then the Chamber one day before the final pre-trial conference to reach a decision in respect of this motion, so that the pre-trial conference could be conducted in the knowledge of how this motion has been determined. So with that slight plea, I invite, Mr. Saxon, your observations whether it would be really just not fair and practical to ask for a response to the motion by the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution understands now the urgency of -- that the Chamber receive a motion -- a response from the Prosecution prior to the pre-trial conference. However, with the great respect, I would ask the Chamber to consider whether it would give the Prosecution until 1300 hours on the 11th of April to file its response. I'm simply afraid that the quality of our response will not be to a high standard if we attempt to file by 4.00 on the 10th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In the anticipation that my colleagues will volunteer to work through the night to accommodate you, Mr. Saxon, you may have until 1300 hours on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: May we thank you for coming, and in particular may we acknowledge the burden this procedure has placed on those who have been here translating what we have been saying. The delivery of six decisions, even though in abbreviated form in a form like this, clearly places great demands on people. It's because we have been appointed so near the commencement of the trial and there were no less than 23 motions to be dealt with, there are now 24, some of those have already been dealt with by these decisions and the decisions last Friday, and it is only by means such as this that we can keep up with the time pressures to try and ensure that both parties have a clear understanding of where we are by the commencement of the trial. Thank you all. We now adjourn.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.30 p.m.
